chapter.name: Elections
chapter.blurb: Why elections matter, electoral systems, election laws and delimitation, the Election Commission, political parties and defection, and challenges to free and fair elections.

concepts.name: Why elections matter: direct and indirect elections
concepts.description: The importance of regular elections, direct and indirect elections in India and the meaning of psephology.
concepts.idea: Regular elections let citizens choose and hold accountable those who make decisions on their behalf.
concepts.rule: Members of the Lok Sabha, Vidhan Sabha and local bodies are directly elected every five years. The President, Vice President and members of the Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected. Psephology is the scientific study of elections (Greek psephos, pebble).
concepts.example: A class representative cannot continue for ever without a fresh election, and a government cannot continue beyond its term without a mandate.

questions.q: Give two examples each of direct and indirect elections in India.
questions.a: Direct: Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha (also local bodies). Indirect: President, Vice President and Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: Can we exercise a real choice if only one political party contests an election? Explain.
questions.a: No. A choice needs more than one option. Elections need competition so people can compare and choose their representatives.

questions.q: Explain why elections are called the process of exercising the right to vote and fulfilling the responsibility of a citizen.
questions.a: By voting, citizens exercise their right to choose those who decide on their behalf and fulfil a civic responsibility. Elections also hold representatives accountable to the people.

questions.q: Which situation shows that an election is not meaningful?
questions.a: only one party is allowed to contest
o: only one party is allowed to contest

questions.q: Distinguish between direct and indirect elections with an example each.
questions.a: In a direct election voters directly elect their representative, as for the Lok Sabha. In an indirect election representatives elect officials, as the President and the Rajya Sabha members are chosen by elected members of legislatures.

questions.q: Explain why periodic elections are essential for a democracy.
questions.a: They let people choose their representatives, replace non-performing ones, keep governments accountable and preserve the mandate of the people. Without them the government could continue without consent.

questions.q: Ravi says once elected, a government can rule as long as it likes. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Governments are elected for a fixed term, usually five years, and must seek the people's mandate again through periodic elections.

questions.q: Complete the statement "Elections are important in a democracy because ..." with two reasons.
questions.a: They give every citizen an equal voice in choosing the government, and they ensure that representatives are accountable to the people.

concepts.name: Electoral systems: FPTP and proportional representation
concepts.description: The First-Past-The-Post system, proportional representation with single transferable vote, and the bicameral structure of legislatures in six states.
concepts.idea: An electoral system decides how votes are converted into seats.
concepts.rule: India chose the plurality (First-Past-The-Post) system for the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha. The Rajya Sabha, President, Vice President and Vidhan Parishad use proportional representation by the single transferable vote. Six states have a bicameral legislature with a Vidhan Parishad and a Vidhan Sabha.
concepts.example: Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh have two houses.

questions.q: Describe the steps of counting and transferring votes in the single transferable vote system.
questions.a: Voters mark their preferences. First preference votes are counted and candidates who reach the quota (minimum votes needed) are elected. The candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and those votes go to the next preference. This continues until the required number of candidates is elected.
s: Quota and election of those reaching it

questions.a: The way seats are allocated differs, and each country chooses the system suited to its size and diversity and the kind of representation it wants.

questions.q: Explain the composition and election of the Vidhan Parishad.
questions.a: It is the upper house in the six bicameral states. Its members are elected by members of the Vidhan Sabha and local bodies, by graduates and teachers, and some are nominated by the Governor from fields like art and science. Elections use proportional representation by a single transferable vote.

questions.q: Suppose a constituency election has several candidates. Explain how the winner is decided under FPTP.
questions.a: The candidate who gets the most votes, even without a majority, is declared the winner of that seat.

concepts.name: Election laws and delimitation of constituencies
concepts.description: The Representation of the People Acts, electoral offences and corrupt practices, and the delimitation of constituencies.
concepts.idea: Laws and delimitation make elections fair, transparent and equal in representation.
concepts.rule: RPA 1950: allocation of seats, delimitation, electoral rolls and the right of every citizen of 18 or above to vote. RPA 1951: nominations, campaigns, voting, disputes, electoral offences and corrupt practices. Delimitation fixes constituency boundaries under Article 82; there have been four Commissions (1952, 1963, 1973, 2002).
concepts.example: Without delimitation one MP might represent five lakh people and another twenty-five lakh.

questions.q: Who can vote according to the RPA 1950?
questions.a: Every citizen of 18 years or above has the right to vote without discrimination, provided their name is on the electoral roll.

questions.q: Explain the roles of RPA 1950 and RPA 1951 together.
questions.a: RPA 1950 covers allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies, electoral rolls and voting rights. RPA 1951 covers nomination, campaigns, voting procedure, electoral offences and dispute resolution. Together they ensure integrity, transparency and accountability.

questions.q: Why is delimitation important for equal representation?

o: It prevents some MPs representing far more people than others

questions.q: What could happen if there were no delimitation?
questions.a: Some constituencies would have far larger populations than others, so votes and representation would be unequal, defeating the objective of equal representation.

questions.q: Explain how laws and commissions together keep elections fair.
questions.a: The RPA Acts set rules for rolls, nomination, campaigning and disputes; the Delimitation Commission keeps constituencies equal; and the Election Commission enforces the process. Together they keep elections transparent and accountable.

questions.q: Ali says a candidate may promise gifts to voters to win support. Evaluate.

questions.q: Suggest two rules you would make for a school election to keep it fair, based on the Acts.
questions.a: No gifts or promises to buy votes, no appeals based on caste, religion or language, and no help from teachers for candidates.

concepts.name: The Election Commission of India and its functions
concepts.description: The constitutional status of the ECI, its officers, its functions such as electoral rolls, scheduling, registering parties and symbols, and inclusive voting initiatives.
concepts.idea: The ECI is an autonomous constitutional body that supervises, directs and controls the whole election process.
concepts.rule: ECI: autonomous permanent constitutional body established on 25 January 1950 (Articles 324-329). Functions: prepare electoral rolls and conduct Special Intensive Revision, decide election schedule, register parties and allot symbols, ensure free and fair elections. Initiatives: voting from home, ETPBS, cVIGIL.
concepts.example: In 2024 voting from home was extended across India for senior citizens above 85 and persons with 40 per cent benchmark disability.

questions.q: Describe how the ECI prepares the electoral roll.

questions.a: Accessible infrastructure and technology for persons with disabilities, senior citizens, transgender persons and PVTGs; voting from home for those above 85 and PwDs; and ETPBS for service voters.

questions.q: Explain why the ECI's functions ensure free and fair elections.
questions.a: Accurate electoral rolls let every eligible voter vote, a fair schedule considers local conditions, registration of parties and symbols organises the contest, and enforcement and technology such as cVIGIL and inclusive voting keep the process impartial and accessible.

questions.q: Sam says the ECI is a department of the government that follows orders of ministers. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The ECI is an autonomous, permanent constitutional body vested with superintendence, direction and control of elections.

questions.q: You will turn 18 soon. List the steps you would take to register as a voter and to vote on election day.
questions.a: Check eligibility and apply online or through the ECI portal, verify details on the electoral roll, carry valid identity proof, go to the polling station and cast the vote after identity verification.

concepts.name: Political parties, defection and alliances
concepts.description: The role of political parties in elections, the multi-party system, the Anti-Defection Law, recognition of parties and coalitions.
concepts.idea: Political parties present programmes and policies, and the law prevents members from switching sides for personal gain.
concepts.rule: India has a multi-party system. Defection is switching from the party under whose banner one was elected. The Anti-Defection Law (1985, 52nd Amendment) can disqualify a member who voluntarily gives up party membership or votes against the whip. Alliances began in 1967; the Janata Party formed the first coalition government at the Centre in 1977.
concepts.example: Since the late 1990s the NDA and the UPA have been the major alliances.

concepts.name: Challenges to free and fair elections and the importance of voting
concepts.description: Challenges such as misinformation and intimidation, the safeguards of the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs and VVPAT, and why voting matters.
concepts.idea: Free and fair elections face practical challenges that the law, the ECI and active citizens work to overcome.
concepts.rule: Challenges include misinformation, fake news and intimidation. The ECI responds through RPA 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, VVPAT, voter awareness campaigns and technology. Casting a vote is a constitutional right as well as a duty; elections are the soul of democracy.

questions.q: Name two measures used by the ECI to deal with challenges to free and fair elections.
questions.a: The Model Code of Conduct, EVMs and VVPAT, voter awareness campaigns, the RPA Acts and technology such as cVIGIL.

questions.q: Give two reasons why you should vote.
questions.a: To choose my representative, to change a non-performing representative, and to become a responsible citizen.

questions.q: Read the case of Ishani and list three ways the election process was made inclusive and fair.
questions.a: She had registered through the ECI online portal, a wheelchair and volunteers helped her brother, her identity was verified with an alternative document, she saw the VVPAT slip, and voting from home was possible for her 89-year-old grandmother.

questions.q: Which action violates the Model Code of Conduct?
questions.a: offering gifts to voters or using government vehicles for campaigning
o: offering gifts to voters or using government vehicles for campaigning
holding a peaceful rally with the permission of the officers
displaying a manifesto of the party to the public
voting at the polling station on the day of the poll

questions.q: Why must electoral rolls be revised regularly?
questions.a: People die, move or are duplicated, and young people turn 18, so revision ensures every eligible voter is included and no ineligible person is on the roll.

questions.q: Explain the challenges to free and fair elections in India and how they can be met.
questions.a: With over 96.8 crore voters, thousands of polling stations and many parties, misinformation, fake news, intimidation and inaccessibility are challenges. They are met by laws (RPA 1950 and 1951), the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs with VVPAT, awareness campaigns, technology and active citizens.
s: Laws and Model Code of Conduct

questions.q: Vik says one vote does not matter, so voting is not necessary. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Every vote gives an equal voice in choosing the government and holds it accountable. Voting is both a right and a duty, and low participation weakens democracy.

questions.q: Arrange in your order of preference and justify: (a) opportunity to choose my representative, (b) makes me a responsible person, (c) opportunity to change a non-performing representative.
questions.a: For example (a), (c), (b): choosing is the basic right, changing shows accountability, and responsibility follows from participation. Any order with reasons linked to democracy is valid.
